summary.text: Decolonization is the ending of colonialism, the process by which imperial nations establish and dominate foreign territories.
As a movement it began with the American Revolution in 1775, with later waves after the First World War, after the Second World War and after the Cold War.
The United Nations treats self-determination as its core requirement, and a 1960 resolution called colonial foreign rule a violation of human rights.

items.prompt: A small territory's people choose to govern themselves while staying part of a larger country. Can the UN view this as meeting the core requirement?

options.label: No, only a fully separate sovereign state would count
No, unless the empire that held it first collapses
Yes, because the right can be exercised without political independence
Yes, but only after the territory wins a war of independence

items.explain: The UN says the right to self-determination is the core requirement and can be exercised with or without political independence.

items.prompt: A government finds that holding its overseas territories earns little and drains its treasury. Which explanation of decolonization fits?

options.label: Rising education in the colonies led to calls for popular rule
Earlier revolts inspired later ones in other colonies
A shift to wage labor created a larger bourgeois class
Colonizing paid off less and the empire cost more to keep

items.explain: One explanation stresses the lower profitability of colonization and the costs of empire.

items.prompt: What opened the door to independence for Spain's American colonies in the early 1800s?

options.label: Spain sold the colonies to Britain in a treaty
Chaos from the Napoleonic Wars cut their direct links to Spain
A slave uprising spread from Saint-Domingue to every colony
The colonies voted to join the Junta of Cadiz for good

items.explain: The Napoleonic Wars cut the direct links between Spain and its American colonies, allowing decolonization to begin.

items.prompt: A writer says she is decolonizing her own mind, shedding the belief that her people are lesser. Which use of the term is this?

options.label: Intellectual decolonization from the colonizers' thinking
Political decolonization through sovereign statehood
Economic decolonization through new trade routes
Military decolonization through a rebel victory

items.explain: The term is also used for intellectual decolonization from the colonizers' ideas that made the colonized feel inferior.

items.prompt: A teacher says the movement to break away from distant imperial rulers first appeared in North America. Which event is she describing?

options.label: The Haitian Revolution against France
The Napoleonic Wars across Europe
The American Revolution against the British Empire
The collapse of the Soviet Union

items.explain: Decolonization as a movement is described as beginning with the American Revolution against the British Empire.

items.prompt: Debaters drafting a constitution for a newly independent country lean on individualism and liberalism. Whose theories are these?

options.label: Marxist analysis of wage labor and class
Enlightenment social and political theory
Diffusion theory of earlier revolts
Modern critiques of Indigenous erasure

items.explain: Enlightenment theories such as individualism and liberalism were central to debates about constitutions in newly independent countries.

beats.title: Why empires let go
beats.hook: Empires that once seemed permanent ended in two centuries, and scholars still disagree about why.

beats.prompt: Two empires each fight rebels in a faraway colony, one in the 19th century and one in the 20th. Which is more likely to have strong backing from its own public?
beats.explain: In the 19th century colonial powers had strong political will and regional support; in the 20th century they faced apathetic publics and hostile superpowers.

choices.label: The 19th-century empire, with strong political will behind it
Both equally, since empires always have loyal publics
choices.feedback: It tempts as a simple rule, but the explanation says conditions changed between the centuries.

choices.label: The 20th-century empire, whose public sees colonies as a prize
choices.feedback: It tempts because empires look strong, but by then publics were apathetic and holding colonies was often seen as a burden.

beats.prompt: Put these moments of decolonization in order

items.label: Thirteen North American colonies declare independence from Britain
Latin American independence wars begin with a revolt in La Paz
Palau becomes independent and Hong Kong and Macau are handed over

beats.explain: The United States came in 1776, Haiti in 1804, the Latin American wars in 1809, and the last wave after the Cold War.

right.label: Lower profitability and the costs of empire

paragraphs.heading: What the word means
paragraphs.text: Decolonization is the end of colonialism, which is when imperial nations take over and rule foreign lands, often across the sea. People disagree about exactly what the word means and how to use it. Some scholars focus on independence movements in colonies and on the fall of global empires. David Strang says it is achieved when a territory becomes a sovereign state formally recognised by other nations, or is fully merged into an existing state. The United Nations puts the right to self-determination at its heart and says this right can be used with or without full independence.

paragraphs.heading: Waves of independence
paragraphs.text: As a push for colonies to break free from the countries that ruled them, decolonization began in 1775 with the American Revolution against the British Empire. During the Napoleonic Wars, revolution in Haiti, independence wars in Spanish America and Brazil's split from Portugal brought decolonization to the French, Spanish and Portuguese empires. Big waves followed after the First World War and after the Second, when many countries won independence in the years that came after. A last wave came after the Cold War, as the Soviet Union collapsed, Palau became independent, and Hong Kong and Macau were handed over. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies won independence from Western powers, yet seventeen territories are still classed by the UN as non-self-governing.

paragraphs.heading: The first breakaways
paragraphs.text: The first colonies to break away were Britain's thirteen in North America, which declared independence in 1776 as the United States and beat Britain in the Revolutionary War. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue on Hispaniola, a revolt in 1789 and a slave uprising in 1791 led to Haiti's independence in 1804. When Napoleon invaded Spain, the turmoil cut Spain's direct links with its American colonies. Spain's grip on their trade was the main reason many chose independence, and the wars began with a revolt in La Paz, Bolivia, in 1809. For about fifteen years royalists and rebels fought across South America and Mexico, and many countries declared independence.

paragraphs.heading: Why it spread
paragraphs.text: Scholars give several reasons why anti-colonial movements spread. One view says that more education in the colonies led people to demand rule by the people. Marxist accounts point to economic shifts toward wage labour and a growing middle class, while others see each revolution inspiring the next. Some stress that colonies became less profitable and empires more costly. Others note that by the 20th century colonial powers faced indifferent publics at home, hostile superpowers and fewer local allies, so holding on to colonies came to feel like a burden.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas and rights
paragraphs.text: Many historians trace the ideas behind independence movements to the Age of Enlightenment. Enlightenment theories such as individualism and liberalism shaped debates over the constitutions of newly independent countries. Today's decolonial scholars criticise those same ideas for erasing Indigenous ways of knowing and for failing to give liberty, equality and dignity to marginalised and Indigenous people. In 1960 a UN General Assembly resolution described colonial rule by foreigners as a breach of human rights.

paragraphs.heading: Minds, cultures and today
paragraphs.text: The word can also mean freeing the mind from colonisers' ideas that made colonised people feel inferior. Early studies came in the 1960s and 1970s, and Frantz Fanon, a writer from Martinique, set out in The Wretched of the Earth (1961) many themes later writers took up. Later work looked at the economic inequality colonialism left behind and at the destruction of cultures, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's Decolonising the Mind (1986) examined its effects on culture and language. These questions are still raised today: Indigenous peoples under settler colonialism keep calling for decolonization and self-determination, and in the Americas and South Africa the debate often goes by the name decoloniality.
